claims.text: The target material is bulk, polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr produced by sintering.
The target specimen contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen as interstitial oxygen.
Sintered HfNbTaTiZr has processing-induced defects and grain boundaries relevant to its properties.

A predictive model can be constructed using atomistic simulation or machine learning to include oxygen-interstitial scattering, grain-boundary scattering, and temperature-dependent phonon interactions.
Quantum and defect scattering predominate in HfNbTaTiZr over the nearly 0–200 K regime.
Enhanced phonon scattering and defect interactions are significant in HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
Oxygen interstitials and grain boundaries mediate scattering processes that affect conductivity.
Atomic-size mismatch produces lattice distortions that contribute to conductivity-relevant scattering.
Including defect and oxygen-interstitial scattering captures charge-carrier and phonon transport contributions absent from ideal-crystal predictions.
Defect-induced carrier localization is an important low-temperature transport mechanism in this alloy.
Phonon-defect interactions are an important high-temperature transport mechanism in this alloy.
The defect-inclusive model will predict measured conductivity within approximately 5–10% across both specified temperature regimes.
The defect-inclusive model will significantly outperform conventional defect-free analytical models.
Conventional defect-free analytical models can have conductivity errors greater than 20% for this material.
Existing analytical approaches assume perfect, defect-free crystals and omit scattering from oxygen and processing-induced defects.
The proposed model is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with microstructures and oxygen content near 1 wt.% and may not transfer directly to substantially different oxygen contents or microstructures.
Prediction accuracy may vary with defect density, oxygen distribution, and processing history.

The hypothesis is falsified if the model's mean conductivity error exceeds 15% across the tested temperatures or if its error reduction relative to conventional models is not statistically significant.
